title: The code close
hookLine: a shared way of life for a scattered people

cards: A small apartment, at evening. A family stands for the Ardas, hands folded, the youngest peeking at the others to see when to bow.
Half a world away, a crowded gurdwara does the same, at a different hour of the same turning planet. They've never met. They don't share a climate, a currency, or a first language for their children.
But they stand at the same words, bow at the same moment, and hand out karah prashad the same way, into cupped hands. That sameness didn't happen by accident.

teach.h: WHO IS A SIKH, TO HUMILITY AND JOY.
teach.b: Flip back through this block like a photo album. It opened with a plain question: who is a Sikh?
Then the daily banis, rising early, the sangat and the gurdwara: how the Granth is opened and rested, what may be sung, how the hukam is taken. Readings, karah prashad, katha. No caste, no charms.

Daswandh. The turban, a child's naming, the wedding and remarriage, simple funerals. Then amrit: who gives it, what is promised, what happens when it's broken, and the penance that mends it as service.
The Guru Panth, the Akal Takht and the jathedars, the Takhts one by one, the Sarbat Khalsa, the older rehatnamas, and why a code was written down at all.
Then the body and the day: kesh, turbans, the kirpan and the law, kara and kangha, food, a clear mind, faithfulness at home.
And last, the spirit it's kept in: love, return, children, work, your own rehat, humility and joy. What does it add up to?

teach.h: A SCATTERED PEOPLE, A SHARED SHAPE.
teach.b: Sikhs live today in countries around the world, and a scattered people could easily have drifted into separate customs.

The code gives them a shared shape instead: the same morning prayers, the same articles, the same ceremonies, the same way of serving karah prashad. And a line in the Ardas holds the scattering inside it.

teach.h: THE ARDAS: WHEREVER THE KHALSA IS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: wherever the Khalsa is, there may there be protection and grace. Wherever. The prayer assumes a people spread out, and asks for them all at once.

teach.h: ONE WAY, KEPT IN MANY PLACES.
teach.b: And it isn't the whole story: the panth also holds many orders and schools, each with its own emphasis. That's where the path goes next.

how: Sikhs in different countries follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada as a shared reference, so the daily prayers, the five articles, the ceremonies and the serving of karah prashad look alike from one gurdwara to the next.

o: a shared way of life for a people spread worldwide
the last rule added to the code by the Gurus
a single gurdwara that rules over all the rest

games.q: two families in two cities who have never met stand for the evening Ardas. what makes their prayer look alike?
o: a shared code and a shared prayer.
games.why: the Rehat Maryada and the Ardas give a scattered people one shape: the same words, the same bow, the same prashad.

practice: Choose one small thing from this block: a morning remembrance, a clear drink, a promise kept, a good word instead of a score.
Picture people around the world keeping their own version of it today, in other cities and other hours, and hold yours as something shared with them.

wordCard.voice: The code close. The Sikh Rehat Maryada gives a scattered people a shared way of life, and the Ardas asks for protection and grace wherever the Khalsa is. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: path, way; also the Sikh community as a whole, the panth.

carryVoice: Your line: one way, many places. Wherever you keep it, you aren't keeping it alone. Block closed.
